problem: Prior VLN work either assumes limited use of environment knowledge or relies on coarse aggregate metrics (SR/SPL) that hide why agents fail. This dissertation targets both method design across information settings and the lack of fine-grained evaluation.
motivation: Embodied agents should perceive scenes, objects and events and communicate in a human-like way, so VLN is used as a testbed for multimodal representation learning. Current evaluation does not diagnose model capabilities, which limits understanding of robustness in real-world use.
key_idea: Study VLN under two information settings (global information awareness in known environments, local information reliance in unseen ones) and propose a fine-grained framework to diagnose and benchmark VLN models.
insight: Only the abstract is available, so no ablations or analysis can be cited. The abstract implies that the information available to the agent (global vs local) shapes method design, and that fine-grained evaluation exposes shortcomings hidden by aggregate metrics.
method: Global information awareness setting: agents operate in known environments and exploit global environment information.
Local information reliance setting: agents rely on heuristics derived from data in unseen environments.
Fine-grained evaluation framework: diagnoses and benchmarks VLN models to address shortcomings of current evaluation.
